scope1_writeRawBypass.inFlightFrames: frames already queued in the kernel/socket buffer before revocation are unavoidably delivered (TCP); they were authorized at write time and every journaled frame re-passes _mayDeliver at write time. No post-revocation frame is ever WRITTEN. Synchronous single-threaded wiring means revocation cannot interleave inside publish()/handleSubscribe().
scope1_writeRawBypass.suppressionAnalysis: _resetOne failure modes only reduce to close-without-reset when the transport is already dead (bytes undeliverable anyway) or the device is inactive on the non-bypass path; the bypass path has no authorization-dependent suppression. Duplication is impossible: _resetOne is fully synchronous, resetting flag is set before any write, and dropDevice closes immediately after the single write.

structuralCompleteness.composition: _authority = JSON [replayEpoch, serviceId, sorted grantedScopes, sorted true-grant keys, sha256 of sorted per-conversation owner tuples (conversationId, namespace, identity, epoch, projectId)]
structuralCompleteness.deliveryDecisionInputs: frame delivery depends on: device active (null authority -> drop), scopes, grants, conversation existence, project binding. Every input is inside the composition — verified row by row in C4/C5.
structuralCompleteness.singleThreaded: authorization transitions are synchronous transactions (device-store persists then notifies in the same call stack); no async gap exists in the subscribe path (admission + handleSubscribe synchronous), and mutations re-verify liveness at commit time (commitAdmission + listener live re-check, both reading the in-place-mutated record).
structuralCompleteness.ownerRevisionEcho: frame ownerRevision is echoed state, not an authorization input; the mobile client's authorizeResource mirror (src/remote/events.ts + demo wiring) likewise ignores ownerRevision for the grant decision — the removal of exact-equality re-check is coherent on both sides.

scope3_epochPersistence.verdict: sound — the theorized regression window does not exist

keyFacts.ownerEpochConstantOne: EMPIRICAL (E3): epochFor NEVER increments an existing entry; the identity string itself carries workspaceEpoch, so every authority transition is a NEW identity starting at 1. Distinct epoch values observed across 200 identities: [1]. An evicted-then-reappearing identity returning epoch 1 is therefore IDENTICAL to it never having been evicted — there is nothing to regress from.
keyFacts.signatureReplayIndependent: signed-request replay protection binds device.replayEpoch (per-device, in the signature message), never the owner epoch. The owner epoch only partitions mutation idempotency keys and feeds commitAdmission's owner-roll detection.
keyFacts.noncePersistence: EMPIRICAL (E4): nonces AND timestampFloor persist in remote-devices.json; a validly-signed request accepted pre-restart is rejected as request_replayed post-restart within the skew window. Even if epochs COULD regress, signature replay would remain impossible.
keyFacts.timestampFloorStrict: EMPIRICAL (E5): a freshly-signed request with timestamp below the persisted floor is rejected (request_replayed at the nonce layer) even inside the 60s skew window
keyFacts.epochBumpInvalidation: EMPIRICAL (E6): bumpReplayEpoch invalidates all prior-epoch signatures (signature_invalid)

scope3_epochPersistence.persistenceChangeAssessment: the in-scope epochs-persistence change is harmless-but-vestigial hardening: since values can only ever be 1, persisting them changes no outcome. Eviction correctness itself (oldest-first, capacity 4096, persist per insertion) verified (E2: sizeBefore=4096, firstEvicted=true, reappearedEpoch=1). No severity.
honestResiduals: IdempotencyStore refuses all NEW mutation keys permanently once 4096 records accumulate (no eviction) — pre-existing, out of diff scope, availability-only
contract skew is 60s (not 5 minutes as the brief suggested); retention 180s — the replay surface is smaller than assumed, and entirely covered by nonce persistence

findings.title: res.write()===false misread as write failure — spurious stream close under backpressure
findings.location: server/remote/event-stream.mjs _writeBytes (in-scope refactor consolidated the pattern; identical semantics pre-existed in _write and the keepalive path)
findings.evidence: probe5 R2/R3 + Node semantics reproduction (1MB write returns false yet all 1048581 bytes including the trailing marker are delivered): write()===false is a backpressure hint, the bytes are still queued. Consequence: an ordinary publish whose socket buffer exceeds the 16KB HWM — far below the 1MB budget — closes the stream even though the frame was successfully queued. Security impact: none — the frame bytes are delivered before close, the revocation reset is likewise already queued (so the revocation-notice contract is not weakened), integrity is enforced by client-side signature+position verification, and pre-close frames remain journaled for replay. Impact is availability-only: streams may die spuriously on slow links (Tailscale) or frame bursts, requiring client resubscribe.
findings.reproduction: probe5-results.json R2/R3 — backpressured publish delivered the frame (ordinaryFrameDelivered=1) but the subscriber was closed before revocation arrived; direct Node repro in review transcript
findings.disposition: non-blocking; inherited semantics, correct fix is to honor backpressure (drain-aware) or drop the write()===false close condition, but not required for acceptance of this diff

observationsNotFindings: Owner-epoch persistence is vestigial (values can only be 1) — harmless hardening, not a defect
